questions.html:
A binary relation $\mathrm{R}$ over a set $\mathrm{A}$ is called a "GO Relation" if for all $\mathrm{x}, \mathrm{y}, \mathrm{z}$ $\in A$, if $x R y$ and $x R z$, then $y R z$.

Which of the following is/are true about a relation $\mathrm{R}?$

options.html: If $R$ is a reflexive and GO relation then $R$ is symmetric.
If $R$ is a reflexive and GO relation then $R$ is transitive.
If $R$ is a GO relation then $R$ is reflexive.
If $R$ is an equivalence relation then $R$ is a GO relation.

questions.solution:
Answer: Not available

Source solution 1 (score: 8)

Detailed Video Solution: Video Solution with Complete Analysis (Click HERE)

A binary relation $\mathrm{R}$ over a set $\mathrm{A}$ is called a Euclidean relation if for all $\mathrm{x}$, $y, z \in A$, if $x R y$ and $x R z$, then $y R z$. For example, the $\equiv k$ relation is Euclidean over $\mathbb{Z}$, but the $\leq$ relation over $\mathbb{N}$ is not.

Let $\mathrm{R}$ be an arbitrary binary relation over some set $\mathrm{A}$.

We can easily prove that $R$ is an equivalence relation if and only if it is reflexive and Euclidean.

questions.html:
A binary relation $\mathrm{R}$ over a set $\mathrm{A}$ is called surjective if the following statement is true about $\mathrm{R}:$

$\forall \mathrm{b} \in \mathrm{A} . \exists \mathrm{a} \in \mathrm{A} . \mathrm{aRb}$

Which of the following statements is(are) true?

options.html: A binary relation $\mathrm{R}$ over a set $\mathrm{A}$ is an equivalence relation if $\mathrm{R}$ is surjective, symmetric, and transitive.
If a binary relation $\mathrm{R}$ over a set $\mathrm{A}$ is an equivalence relation then $\mathrm{R}$ is surjective.
If a binary relation $\mathrm{R}$ over a set $\mathrm{A}$ is reflexive then $\mathrm{R}$ is surjective.
If a binary relation $\mathrm{R}$ over a set $\mathrm{A}$ is surjective then $\mathrm{R}$ is reflexive.

questions.solution:
Answer: Not available

Source solution 1 (score: 9)

Detailed Video Solution: https://youtu.be/CgbRXyhMSfM?t=40&feature=shared

A binary relation $\mathrm{R}$ over a set $\mathrm{A}$ is an equivalence relation if and only if $\mathrm{R}$ is surjective, symmetric, and transitive.

NOTE that Surjective function means that for every element $x$ there is some element $y$ such that $yRx$, Not $xRy.$ So, it is like, every element $x$ has at least one pre-image. 

Matrix Representation of Surjective Relation:

By the definition of Surjective relation, we can say that NO column must be empty, But rows can be empty. 

For example, If base set $\{ a,b,c \}$ then the relation $R = \{ (a,a), (a,b), (a,c) \}$ is Surjective, But rows of $b,c$ are empty in the matrix representation.

Let $\mathrm{R}$ and $\mathrm{T}$ be binary relations over the same set $\mathrm{A}$. We'll say that $\text{R}$ is "no stronger than" $\text{T}$ if the following statement is true:
$$
\forall a \in \mathrm{A} . \forall \mathrm{b} \in \mathrm{A} .(\mathrm{aRb} \rightarrow \mathrm{aTb})
$$
Let $\mathrm{R}$ and $\mathrm{T}$ be binary relations over the same set $\mathrm{A}$ where $\mathrm{R}$ is "no stronger than" $\text{T}.$

Then which of the following is/are true?

options.html: If $\text{R}$ is an equivalence relation, then $\text{T}$ is an equivalence relation.
If $\mathrm{T}$ is an equivalence relation, then $\mathrm{R}$ is an equivalence relation.
If $\text{R}$ is a reflexive relation, then $\text{T}$ is a reflexive relation.
If $\mathrm{T}$ is a reflexive relation, then $\mathrm{R}$ is a reflexive relation.

Given-:

$\forall a \in \mathrm{A} . \forall \mathrm{b} \in \mathrm{A} .(\mathrm{aRb} \rightarrow \mathrm{aTb}) $  is $TRUE$

$(\mathrm{aRb} \rightarrow \mathrm{aTb}) $  $\rightarrow$    $T$ 

    $T$         $T$        $\rightarrow$    $T$ 

    $F$         $T$        $\rightarrow$    $T$ 

    $F$         $F$        $\rightarrow$    $T$ 

Mean, element which are in $R$ is also in $T$

But, elements which are in $T$ are not necessary to be in R

$So$, 

$R$ is "no stronger than" $T$ means that $R$ is a subset of $T$. 

$Now$ $lets$ $check$ $options$,

 

Option($C$), If $R$ is a reflexive relation, then $T$ is a reflexive relation. ($True$)

Because, All elements of $R$ is also in $T$ and $R$ and $T$ define on same set (i.e $A$)

and $R$ contains all elements required for reflexivity on set $A$. So $T$ is also Reflexive.

 

Option($D$) Not always $TRUE$

Let $A$ $=$ {$a,b,c$}

Let $T$ $=$ {$(a,a),(b,b),(c,c)$} and $R$ $=$ {$(b,b),(c,c)$}

 

Option($A$) Not always $TRUE$

Let $A$ $=$ {$a,b,c$}

Let $R$ $=$ {$(a,a),(b,b),(c,c)$} and $T$ $=$ {$(a,a),(b,b),(c,c),(a,b)$}

 

Option($B$) Not always $TRUE$

Let $A$ $=$ {$a,b,c$}

Let $T$ $=$ {$(a,a),(b,b),(c,c)$} and $R$ $=$ {$(b,b),(c,c)$}

 

So, Option $(C)$ is Correct only.

questions.html:
Let $\text{A, B}$ be two finite, non-empty sets, with cardinality of $\text{A, B}$ as $m, n$ respectively.

Let $\mathrm{f}: \mathrm{A} \rightarrow \mathrm{B}$ be a function with domain $\mathrm{A}$ and co-domain $\mathrm{B}$. Let $r$ be the cardinality of range of $f.$

We define a relation $\mathrm{R}$ on $\mathrm{A}$, defined by $(x, y) \in \mathrm{R} \Leftrightarrow \mathrm{f}(x)=\mathrm{f}(y)$.

Which of the following statements is true?

options.html: $\mathrm{R}$ is not an equivalence relation.
$\mathrm{R}$ is an equivalence relation having $r$ equivalence classes.
$\mathrm{R}$ is an equivalence relation having $m$ equivalence classes.
$\mathrm{R}$ is an equivalence relation having $n$ equivalence classes.

questions.html:
A binary relation $R$ over a set $A$ is called total iff for any $x \in A$ and $y \in A$, at least one of $xRy$ or $yRx$ is true.

Which of the following is/are true?

options.html: A binary relation $\mathrm{R}$ over a set $\mathrm{A}$ is a total order iff it is a partial order and it is total.
Every total relation is reflexive.
If a relation $\mathrm{S}$ is total $\&$ symmetric, then $\mathrm{S}$ is an equivalence relation.
Every total relation is transitive.

questions.solution:
Answer: A, B, C

Source solution 1 (score: 2)

A relation $R$ is total if for any $x, y \in A$, either $xRy$ or $yRx$ is true.

  • A. Total Order Definition: True. A total order is indeed a partial order that is also a total relation.

  • B. Total $\implies$ Reflexive: True. For any $x$, the definition requires $xRx$ or $xRx$, both of which mean $xRx$ must be true.

  • C. Total + Symmetric $\implies$ Equivalence: True.

     

  • Total implies reflexive. Symmetric is given. In a total symmetric relation, $aRb \wedge bRc$ implies $bRa$ and $cRb$. However, for an equivalence relation, transitivity must hold. For total relations, $aRb \wedge bRc \implies aRc$ holds when combined with symmetry.

  • Correct Answer: A, B, and C.
